paragraphs.text: Multiple endocrine neoplasia type V (MEN5) is caused by heterozygous inactivating germline mutations in the MAX gene (Charoenngam et al., 2026). It is mainly characterized by highly penetrant pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma, with pituitary adenoma as a cardinal feature. Parathyroid adenomas and pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors are less common manifestations (Maggacis et al., 2026). Seabrook et al. (2021) concluded that germline MAX mutations are associated with pheochromocytomas, ganglioneuromas, neuroblastomas, pituitary neuroendocrine tumors, possibly parathyroid adenomas, and also chondrosarcoma and lung adenocarcinoma. Charoenngam et al. (2026) noted that the epidemiology, penetrance, and genotype-phenotype associations of MEN5 had not yet been defined.

paragraphs.text: Cardot Bauters et al. (2020) described a family with neural crest-derived tumors. The proband (III-1), a woman, developed neuroblastoma of the broad ligament at 17 months of age, which was treated with surgery, radiation therapy, and chemotherapy. At age 22 years she developed a right pheochromocytoma, a ganglioneuroma at the site of the original neuroblastoma, and an ileal schwannoma. Six years later, she underwent surgery for a left pheochromocytoma associated with a mature ganglioneuroma. At the same time, a well-differentiated leiomyosarcoma arising from the mesosigmoid was removed. Her other recorded findings included hypertension, high normetanephrines, metastases of the leiomyosarcoma, hepatic carcinoma, and uterine leiomyoma; the neuroblastoma, leiomyosarcoma, and hepatic carcinoma were attributed to other causes. Her paternal grandfather (I-1) had bilateral pheochromocytoma at 70 years of age. Before surgery he had urinary normetanephrines 5 times and chromogranin A 3 times the upper limit of normal. Her youngest brother (III-3) presented at age 31 years with cardiomyopathy complicated by Takotsubo syndrome, which led to the diagnosis of bilateral pheochromocytoma. At age 56 years, her paternal uncle (II-3) developed an 11-mm hypervascular nodule in the right adrenal gland. The nodule was clinically silent but strongly took up 18F-DOPA on PET, suggesting a pheochromocytoma or adrenomedullary nodule.

paragraphs.text: Seabrook et al. (2021) reported 2 Australian families. In family A, multiple individuals had pheochromocytoma, including bilateral and metastatic disease. Two children who had not developed pheochromocytoma had neuroendocrine tumors: a paravertebral ganglioneuroma in one and an abdominal neuroblastoma in the other. One family member had acromegaly, and their pheochromocytoma tissue stained positive for growth hormone-releasing hormone on immunohistochemistry. Another, whose pheochromocytomas had been resected, had pituitary enlargement and elevated IGF-1. In family B, the proband had bilateral and metastatic pheochromocytoma, a prolactin-producing pituitary tumor, multigland parathyroid adenomas, chondrosarcoma, and multifocal pulmonary adenocarcinomas.

paragraphs.text: Lian et al. (2024) reported 3 probands with MAX mutations. The proband of family A, a man, was diagnosed with right pheochromocytoma at age 24 years. He had more than a 2-year history of elevated blood pressure and was eventually diagnosed with metachronous bilateral pheochromocytoma. He had elevated plasma norepinephrine and no pituitary abnormalities or other neuroendocrine tumors. The proband of family B, a 34-year-old man, was admitted with bilateral adrenal lesions and was diagnosed with simultaneous bilateral pheochromocytoma. He had no headache, palpitations, or excessive sweating; his plasma catecholamine, metanephrine, and normetanephrine levels were normal, and he had no pituitary or parathyroid abnormalities. The proband of family C, a 64-year-old woman, had a unilateral right pheochromocytoma with occasional paroxysmal headache and elevated plasma norepinephrine. She had no pituitary, neck, or chest abnormalities.

paragraphs.text: Lian et al. (2024) reviewed 109 carriers of germline MAX mutations from 87 families, 6 newly reported and 103 previously reported. Of these, 101 (92.7%) developed pheochromocytoma at a mean age of 32.8 years (range, 13 to 80 years); 59 of the pheochromocytomas were bilateral. Nineteen patients (18.8%) had metastatic disease and 11 (10.9%) had a concomitant thoracic or abdominal paraganglioma. Nine carriers (8.3%) had functional growth hormone- and/or prolactin-secreting pituitary neuroendocrine tumors. Eleven (10.1%) had other neuroendocrine tumors, including primary hyperparathyroidism, neuroblastoma, ganglioneuroblastoma/ganglioneuroma, C-cell hyperplasia, and pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor. Seven had non-neuroendocrine tumors whose relation to the mutation was uncertain.

paragraphs.text: In a kindred with MEN5, Haider et al. (2025) identified a novel heterozygous germline 1-bp deletion (c.228delG) in exon 4 of the MAX gene, predicted to cause a frameshift and a truncated protein (Asn78ThrfsTer92). The propositus had pituitary gigantism due to a mixed growth hormone- and prolactin-secreting macroadenoma and bilateral recurrent pheochromocytomas. The kindred had an extensive history of pheochromocytoma or uncontrolled hypertension and included multiple affected and unaffected carriers.
